newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani markets respond warily to Sharif speech.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani markets respond warily to Sharif speech.

text.p: Pakistan markets reacted cautiously on Monday to Nawaz Sharif's first address to the nation since he became prime minister and analysts said they wanted to see the nuts and bolts of his economic policy.

"There was nothing very surprising about the measures announced," said Rizwan Butt, senior analyst at brokerage house Khadim Ali Shah Bukhari & Co. It remained to be seen whether Sharif could implement the promises he made on Sunday, he added.

In his first televised speech since he took office on February 17, Sharif announced plans to reduce foreign debt by urging overseas Pakistanis to make donations, interest-free loans and open hard currency bank accounts at home.
He also offered returns at market rates for individuals prepared to lend to the government and told foreigners he could provide constitutional guarantees to protect their investments.
Sharif, who has yet to name a cabinet, also said he would cut public spending, except defence, one of its major components.

He announced a freeze in electricity and petrol prices, raised the salaries of junior government employees by 300 rupees ($7.46) a month and pensions by 10 percent, and called for similar increases in the private sector.

The Karachi Stock Exchange 100-share index fell 2.66 percent on Monday as investors, unsure of the impact of Sharif's measures, went ahead with settlement day profit-taking in an over-bought market, traders said.
Jahanzeb Naseer, research head at Jardine Fleming Broking Pakistan, said the rise in salaries and pensions alone would cost the government about four billion rupees.
"It seems Sharif's plans will only work if his scheme to bring in foreign currency deposits takes off," Naseer said.
He said the market's general view was that the scheme could bring in around $1 billion in deposits, but the details would have to be examined before making any reliable estimate.
A foreign banker, who asked not to be named, said paying market-based returns on foreign currency deposits by Pakistani expatriates would be an expensive affair.
Dealers in the foreign exchange kerb market said they expected the rupee to slide against the dollar as investors diverted funds to the scheme, drying up the normal dollar supply.
The rupee opened 0.04 up at 41.16 to the dollar on Monday, but dealers said it would soon fall on fresh dollar demand.

Abid Naqvi, research head at Taurus Securities, said the freeze on petrol and power rates was unlikely to last long. "While Sharif's speech was long on patriotic rhetoric, we found it lacking in concrete economic steps," he added.
Analysts said freezing utility charges could widen the fiscal deficit if public utilities were unable to make anticipated payments to the government as a result.

The International Monetary Fund resumed and expanded a standby loan in December after the caretaker government promised to cut the budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product in 1996/97 (July-June) from 6.3 percent in 1995/96.
The IMF has been anxious to know whether Sharif is fully committed to the targets agreed with the fund.

The Finance Ministry said after Sharif met Pakistan's representative on the IMF board on Sunday that Islamabad's standby agreement remained on track and an IMF mission would visit Islamabad soon to review economic performance.
